title: The Floor That Kept the Dead — Neolithic Çatalhöyük Subfloor Burials (Haddow 2025), Shifting Intra-Building Genetic Kinship Across 1,000 Years (63% to 22%, Yaka 2021 & Yüncü 2025) & Maternal Lineage Ties

teenKit.tldr: Neolithic farmers at Çatalhöyük literally lived on top of their ancestors by burying the dead right under their house floors. Ancient DNA reveals that over 1,000 years, the genetic link between housemates dropped from 63% to 22%, proving houses were shared by social choice rather than just blood.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It completely flips our modern idea of home and family, showing that ancient humans built lasting communities based on shared lives and spaces rather than just DNA.
keyTakeaways: People in Neolithic Anatolia (7,100–6,000 BCE) routinely buried their dead beneath the mudbrick floors where they cooked, slept, and lived.
Genomic time-series data shows that biological kinship inside houses drastically declined over a millennium, dropping from 63% down to 22%.
Maternal lineage ties and special grave goods for female subadults hint at complex, community-driven social structures rather than strict biological nuclear families.

vocab.meaning: The study of human remains and physical layers of earth over time to piece together chronological history.
Genetic material extracted from ancient bones and teeth that allows scientists to track biological family trees.
The custom of placing human corpses directly underneath the foundations or floors of inhabited buildings.
The late Stone Age, marked by the rise of permanent farming villages and towns instead of nomadic hunting.

quiz.question: According to ancient DNA studies over the 1,000-year span at Çatalhöyük, what happened to the genetic kinship of people buried together in the same houses?
options: It completely vanished after the first decade
quiz.explanation: Genomic tracking revealed a major shift over time, showing intra-building genetic kinship plummeted from 63% down to 22%.

quiz.question: How did the residents of Çatalhöyük deal with their dead family or community members?
options: They built massive stone pyramids far away from town
They cremated them and scattered the ashes in rivers
They buried them directly beneath the floors of their living spaces
They left them out in the open fields
quiz.explanation: The defining feature of these Neolithic homes was that daily life happened directly on top of subterranean cemeteries.

quiz.question: What broader sociological shift does the decline in biological kinship within houses suggest?
options: Houses were shared based on social bonds and community rather than just strict blood relations
People completely stopped caring about their ancestors
Families moved houses every single week
Only total strangers were allowed to live together
quiz.explanation: As genetic relatedness dropped over centuries while burial customs stayed the same, it proved that 'family' spaces were defined by shared life, not just DNA.
